The caller then used only selectedCoins[0]. The host now converts the target with atomsToAmount and picks a single coin that covers it; multi-input funding is reported explicitly instead of silently truncated.
findings.impact: Automatic channel funding could fail with a false insufficient-funds result, and multi-coin selection was silently dropped.

repro.expected: A 0.2 MINIMA target selects a coin covering 0.2 MINIMA.
repro.actual: Fixed: the target crosses the boundary as decimal text and one sufficient coin is chosen; multi-input selection raises an explicit error.

fix.approach: Convert the atom target back to decimal MINIMA at the selection boundary and require one coin that covers the target, with an explicit multi-input error.
constraints: Do not drop selected inputs silently.
Never pass an atom integer to a decimal-MINIMA API.
acceptance: A fractional target selects a sufficient single coin.
Multi-input selection fails explicitly.

findings.title: Factory RPCs interpret contributions as atoms instead of decimal amounts
findings.summary: prepareFactory and createFactory used BigInt(requiredString(item, "contributionAmount")), unlike every other host monetary parameter. A decimal fraction was rejected and a whole number meant that many atoms. Both handlers now use rpcAmountToAtoms.
findings.impact: Fractional contributions were rejected and whole numbers were treated as atoms, corrupting totalValue, allocations and escape shares.

repro.expected: A 0.2 MINIMA contribution is accepted as 0.2 MINIMA.
repro.actual: Fixed: both factory paths convert at the RPC boundary.

fix.approach: Convert every participant contribution with rpcAmountToAtoms and cover both the prepared and one-shot factory paths.
constraints: Do not mix atom and decimal contribution paths.
acceptance: Fractional contributions produce atom allocations.
Oversized atom integers are rejected.

findings.title: Inbound HTLC validation compared the proposed state with itself
findings.summary: _handleStateUpdate replaced the persisted pendingHTLCs with the peer-supplied set before verifyStateForCoSign, so validateHtlcSet compared proposed HTLC terms with themselves. Verification now uses the persisted channel; the proposed set is only used for digest/signature construction.
findings.impact: A counterparty could retain an HTLC id while changing its hashlock, timeout, amount or parties and still be co-signed.

repro.expected: Verification receives the persisted HTLC set.
repro.actual: Fixed: verifyState/verifyStateForCoSign receives the original channel.

fix.approach: Validate against the persisted channel and keep the proposed state only for digest construction.
constraints: New HTLC ids remain valid; existing ids may only transition forward.
acceptance: A mutated existing HTLC term is rejected.
A new HTLC is still accepted.

findings.title: Crash recovery could lose the signing watermark after a WOTS signature was released
findings.summary: The double-sign guard was an in-memory watermark plus a pendingProposal field persisted after signing. A crash after signState but before the channel was stored could forget the signed state and allow a different payload at the same sequence. An append-only signing intent is now recorded before the signer is invoked, the signed state is persisted before the ACK, and an unresolved attempt blocks conflicting payloads after restart.
findings.impact: Two conflicting states for one sequence could be signed after a restart.

repro.expected: A durable signing-intent record exists before the signer is invoked and blocks conflicting payloads after restart.
repro.actual: Fixed: beginSigningAttempt runs before prepare/sign; integration persists before ACK.

fix.approach: Persist an append-only signing intent before signing, persist the signed state before the ACK, and block conflicting attempts after restart. Hosts supply a durable journal.
constraints: Never sign two payloads for one sequence.
An attempt with a released signature can never be abandoned.
acceptance: Crash injection after signing cannot produce a conflicting signature.
An identical payload replay is still allowed.

findings.title: The host could issue active VTXOs without verified on-chain backing
findings.summary: createVtxoPool accepted a caller-declared totalCapacity without funding proof, and mintVtxo persisted an active VTXO without verifying pool backing or operator authorization. Pool creation now requires a confirmed, unspent coin covering the capacity; mints are conserved against that backing and stay provisional until the operator co-signs the receipt.
findings.impact: The local ledger could represent transferable liabilities with no on-chain pool coin behind them.

repro.expected: A VTXO becomes active only after confirmed pool backing and the operator receipt.
repro.actual: Fixed: backing is chain-verified, mints are conserved, provisional until the receipt is signed.

fix.approach: Separate provisional issuance from transferable claims; require confirmed backing, conservation and the operator receipt before active.
constraints: Never advertise unbacked VTXOs as redeemable.
Re-verify the backing coin is unspent at mint time.
acceptance: An unfunded pool is rejected.
Capacity above the backing coin is rejected.
Mints stay provisional until co-signed.

findings.title: VTXO exits could be marked complete without proving a payout
findings.summary: completeVtxoExit called markExited with an optional caller txpowId; neither the host nor markExited checked the exit transaction, funding coin, payout or confirmations. Completion now requires a mandatory transaction id and a trusted verifier that confirms owner, amount, token and depth; the VTXO stays exiting otherwise.
findings.impact: The VTXO ledger could report settlement finality with no corresponding payment.

repro.expected: Exit completion requires verified chain evidence.
repro.actual: Fixed: completeVtxoExit requires a verifier and markExited requires a transaction id.

fix.approach: Require a trusted verifier for the exact exit transaction, funding input, owner output, amount/token and depth; keep exiting until verified.
constraints: No caller assertion may finalize an exit.
acceptance: An unverified exit stays exiting.
A verified exit becomes exited.
A wrong owner or shallow confirmation is rejected.

findings.title: Recreating a VTXO pool with the same identity reset its capacity and commitment history
findings.summary: createVtxoPool unconditionally stored a freshly initialized pool under its deterministic id, so repeating the request reset available capacity, epoch and the membership set while earlier VTXOs stayed in the store. Creation is now create-only: an identical repeat returns the existing pool, and different terms are rejected.
findings.impact: Capacity could be re-issued while orphaning the original membership history.

repro.expected: A repeated pool creation never resets capacity, epoch or members.
repro.actual: Fixed: the existing pool is returned (existed:true); conflicting terms are rejected.

fix.approach: Make creation create-only and idempotent for identical terms.
constraints: Never reset capacity, epoch or members through the creation endpoint.
acceptance: A repeat returns the existing pool.
Different terms are rejected.
Capacity and members are unchanged.

findings.title: VTXO refresh could overwrite its own input because the id excluded the epoch
findings.summary: computeVtxoId ignored the epoch, so reusing the mint nonce made the refreshed output id equal to the input id and the host stored the replacement over the consumed record. Replacement ids now include the epoch, and a refresh that would reproduce its input id is rejected.
findings.impact: A consumed VTXO id could become active again, making proof and status history ambiguous.

repro.expected: A refresh always produces a distinct id.
repro.actual: Fixed: epoch is part of replacement ids; same-id refreshes throw.

fix.approach: Include the epoch in replacement ids and reject an output id equal to the input.
constraints: Mint ids stay stable; only replacements carry an epoch.
acceptance: Refreshing with the mint nonce yields a new id.
The consumed record is preserved.

findings.title: Operator receipt signing broke after the first mint into a VTXO pool
findings.summary: Mint roots commit every accumulated pool member, but the receipt payload was verified against a root rebuilt from only the receipt outputs, so the second mint could not be co-signed. Receipts now verify outputs against the pool member set and the pool root.
findings.impact: Issuance and operator authorization diverged after the first mint.

repro.expected: The second mint in a pool prepares a valid receipt.
repro.actual: Fixed: batch verification accepts the authoritative member set.

fix.approach: Verify receipt outputs against the pool member leaves and the pool root; the host passes its authoritative set.
constraints: A receipt must never be verified against a root it supplied itself.
acceptance: Second and later mints co-sign.
An output outside the member set is rejected.

findings.title: Duplicate incoming state updates could consume multiple WOTS key pairs at the same sequence
findings.summary: STATE_UPDATE handling was not serialized per channel, so identical retries each reserved and committed two WOTS leaves. Inbound updates are now serialized per channel and identical (channel, sequence, commitment) retries reuse the recorded ACK instead of signing again.
findings.impact: Signing capacity could be consumed without advancing the channel, and one logical update could yield several ACK signatures.

repro.expected: An identical retry reuses the recorded reply.
repro.actual: Fixed: per-channel serialization plus a reply cache.

fix.approach: Serialize per channel and key replies by sequence+commitment.
constraints: Never reserve a second pair of leaves for one commitment.
acceptance: Identical retries produce one signature.
Both retries receive an ACK.

findings.title: Prepared-signature submissions did not prevent one-time WOTS key reuse
findings.summary: submitPay accepted wallet-supplied update and settlement indices without checking they differ or were previously consumed. It now rejects identical leaves and, when a durable leaf registry is configured, rejects a leaf reused for a different digest.
findings.impact: One WOTS leaf could sign two different transaction digests.

repro.expected: Update and settlement signatures use disjoint, unconsumed leaves.
repro.actual: Fixed: indices must differ and consumed leaves are tracked per digest.

fix.approach: Require disjoint indices and record consumed leaves against their digest.
constraints: A leaf may only ever sign one digest.
acceptance: Equal indices are rejected.
A leaf reused for another digest is rejected.

findings.title: Recreating a liquidity pool could erase its authoritative registry
findings.summary: createLiquidityPool built a fresh empty registry and overwrote any existing pool with the same id. Creation is now create-only: an identical repeat returns the existing manifest and registry, and a different capacity is rejected.
findings.impact: Deposits, allocations, withdrawals and receipts could be erased while positions survived.

repro.expected: A repeated creation preserves the existing registry.
repro.actual: Fixed: existing pools are returned unchanged.

fix.approach: Create-only pool ids with a fresh-registry check.
constraints: Never overwrite a registry through the creation endpoint.
acceptance: Registry survives a repeat.
A conflicting capacity is rejected.

findings.title: Splice-in proposals omitted the additional coin address
findings.summary: proposeSpliceIn accepted a coin id and amount but no address, and the builder wrote an empty address placeholder. The address is now a required parameter, carried into the proposal, and the host resolves and verifies the coin (owner, amount, unspent) before proposing.
findings.impact: The standard splice-in path produced transaction bytes that did not describe the added coin.

repro.expected: A splice-in carrying no address is rejected; a real address is encoded.
repro.actual: Fixed: the builder fails closed and the host verifies the coin.

fix.approach: Require the address, carry it through the proposal, and verify the coin on chain.
constraints: Never serialize a placeholder address.
acceptance: Missing address throws.
The encoded input carries the real address.

findings.title: Liquidity deposits could be marked chain-confirmed without requiring confirmation
findings.summary: The deposit verifier never set requireConfirmed, and evaluateDeposit only gated on confirmation when asked. The host now requires confirmation and a real depth (created vs tip), rejects verifier results that report confirmed:false, and the fallback path fails when depth cannot be established.
findings.impact: An unconfirmed or reorg-prone coin could back an active liquidity position.

repro.expected: Only a coin confirmed at depth backs a position.
repro.actual: Fixed: confirmation and depth are mandatory at every funding check.

fix.approach: Add minConfirmations/chainTip to the deposit contract and require them for liquidity funding.
constraints: Never treat a positive MMR entry as depth.
acceptance: A mempool coin is rejected.
Unknown depth is rejected.
A deep coin is accepted.

findings.title: VTXO transfers and refreshes produced active claims absent from the pool commitment
findings.summary: Minting appended to the pool member set, but transfer and refresh outputs kept single-batch proofs and were stored active without joining it. A pool transition primitive now consumes inputs and adds outputs at a new epoch, and the host applies it before persisting.
findings.impact: Active VTXOs could fail membership verification and existing claims were not anchored.

repro.expected: Transfer/refresh outputs are committed by the pool.
repro.actual: Fixed: transitionPoolMembers consumes inputs, adds outputs and republishes the root.

fix.approach: Add an atomic membership transition and use it for transfer and refresh.
constraints: A consumed id can never re-enter the set.
Each transition publishes a new epoch root.
acceptance: Outputs verify against the pool.
Consumed inputs leave the set.
Receipts prepare after the transition.

findings.title: A unilateral VTXO exit could alter the remaining pool root and epoch
findings.summary: The individual-exit branch returned before asserting the successor commitment root or epoch, so an exit could leave a residual pool whose membership matched no published state. Both ports are now preserved in every holder exit branch.
findings.impact: Holders could lose proof continuity after another holder exited.

repro.expected: An individual exit preserves STATE(100) and STATE(101).
repro.actual: Fixed: the exit branch asserts both are unchanged.

fix.approach: Assert root and epoch preservation inside the exit branch, before any RETURN.
constraints: The cooperative branch keeps its monotone epoch rule.
acceptance: Every holder exit branch carries both assertions.

findings.title: VTXO on-chain spending helpers broadcast without required proofs
findings.summary: Anchor, per-share exit and owner-pool transactions treated coin/script proofs as optional and broadcast an empty witness. All three now refuse to broadcast unless proofs are supplied.
findings.impact: Malformed recovery transactions could be produced and submitted.

repro.expected: Broadcasting without proofs is rejected.
repro.actual: Fixed: assertBroadcastProofs gates every broadcast path.

fix.approach: Require proofs for every spending input before broadcasting.
constraints: Offline draft generation may still omit them.
acceptance: Each helper throws without proofs.

findings.title: Funding activation did not consistently wait for chain confirmations
findings.summary: The receiver checked confirmation depth, but the initiator marked a channel active on mere observation and the factory finalizer committed immediately after submission. Both now require depth; a channel or factory whose funding is not confirmed stays opening.
findings.impact: Operational channels or factories could rest on unconfirmed funding.

repro.expected: Activation requires the funding coin at depth.
repro.actual: Fixed: both paths gate on confirmations (default 1).

fix.approach: Apply one finality rule: submitted → observed → confirmed → active.
constraints: Submission is not confirmation.
acceptance: Shallow funding stays opening.
Deep funding activates.

findings.title: KISSVM CHECKSIG ignores its documented data and signature arguments
findings.summary: Minima documents and implements CHECKSIG(public_key data signature): exactly three HEX parameters, verified as TreeKey.verify(data, signature). The SDK evaluator ignored args[1]/args[2] and verified the witness signature over the transaction digest. TypeScript now enforces the reference semantics (tree signature, or a flat WOTS signature over the supplied data) and Rust/WASM does the same for the flat form; both reject 0/1-argument forms, zero-length operands and non-hex operands.
findings.impact: Detached certificates could not be authenticated, so a contestable factory escape (OMN-058) was unimplementable. Scripts that passed locally under the witness-only form would have failed on a real node.

repro.expected: CHECKSIG(pk data sig) verifies the supplied signature over the supplied data.
repro.actual: Fixed: the evaluator verifies the supplied data and signature. The parity suite measures TS against the Rust/WASM artifact on the same fixtures; the node leg is scripts/kissvm-node-parity.mjs.

fix.approach: Implement the reference three-argument form while keeping SIGNEDBY as the witness path, and prove TS/Rust agreement with shared fixtures generated from real keys.
constraints: Do not silently keep the current meaning under the documented signature.
Cover both the witness path and the detached path with real signatures.
acceptance: CHECKSIG(pk data sig) returns true only for a valid signature over data.
A stale or foreign certificate fails.
The witness cannot change the verdict.
0/1-argument and zero-length forms are rejected.
TypeScript and Rust/WASM agree on every supported fixture.

findings.title: The initiator discards the peer ERROR frame, so a rejected open reports only acknowledged=false
findings.source: live runs: omnia-open-noncustodial.mjs against Hawk v0.2.12 and v0.3.0
findings.summary: The wire protocol defines an ERROR message carrying payload.error, and the responder sends it with a precise reason. requestPeerReply does receive it, but submitOpenChannel reduces the reply to acknowledged = reply.type === 'ACK' and drops the payload; the integration router has no ERROR branch at all, so the frame is not surfaced anywhere.
findings.impact: Every peer-side rejection is opaque to the caller and to the operator log. In this run the actual cause (funding coin not on chain) only became visible after instrumenting the stream layer on the initiator. Support and automation cannot distinguish a rejected proposal from a lost one without patching the SDK.

repro.expected: The submit result or an observation record carries the responder's reason.
repro.actual: Submit returns { success: true, acknowledged: false } with no reason; nothing is logged unless OMNIA_DEBUG is on, and even then only "[omnia-stream] recv ERROR" with no payload.
evidence: packages/omnia/src/integration.ts: _sendError sends payload { error: reason } from 10 call sites
packages/omnia/src/integration.ts: the inbound router switches on CHANNEL_PROPOSAL/STATE_UPDATE/... but has no ERROR case
packages/omnia/src/stream.ts: debug logging prints the message type only
temporary logging-only instrumentation showed: {"error":"acceptChannel failed: Error: Funding coin 0x68778de3... not found on chain"}

fix.approach: Preserve the reason end to end: return it on the submit result (for example acknowledged:false with peerError), include it in the operation record and the observation stream, and handle ERROR explicitly in the integration router so first-contact and routed messages both surface the payload.
constraints: Do not change the ERROR wire format or the reply-matching rules (channelId + nonce).
Do not turn a rejection into a thrown exception where callers already branch on acknowledged.
Do not log secrets from the payload; the reason is a short string.
acceptance: A rejected proposal yields the responder reason to the caller and in the observation record.
The canary can assert on the reason without instrumenting node_modules.

findings.title: Splice successor selection matches on address, token and amount only
findings.source: security audit OMN-NEW-006, verified against source at 8fa26907
findings.summary: observeSpliceSuccessor picks the first unspent coin whose address, token and amount match. Nothing binds the candidate to the splice transaction that created it or to the expected state transition, and the first match wins rather than treating ambiguity as an error.
findings.impact: Two same-value coins at the same script address (a common shape for channel funding addresses) can make the host adopt the wrong coin as the spliced channel. Downstream operations then reference a coin the channel does not control.

repro.expected: The successor is identified by provenance (txid/output index) or ambiguity is rejected.
repro.actual: coins.find(...) on address+token+amount returns the first candidate.
evidence: fix proposed in PR #218 (ambiguous successor is an error)
packages/omnia-splice/src/successor.ts:83 — const candidate = coins.find((coin) => !coin.spent && address && tokenid && amount)

fix.approach: Accept an expected txid/output reference derived from the splice transaction, or read the successor from the spends of the predecessor coin. If more than one candidate matches, fail as ambiguous instead of choosing.
constraints: Do not silently pick a candidate when several match.
Keep the bounded polling and confirmation semantics.
acceptance: Duplicate same-value coins at the address produce an ambiguity error, not a silent pick.
The correct successor is still found in the single-candidate case.

findings.title: Router rollback cannot release HTLCs early and reports failure as if liquidity were returned
findings.source: security audit OMN-NEW-009, verified against source at 8fa26907
findings.summary: On a failed multi-hop payment the router calls timeoutHTLC on each still-pending lock and swallows every error. timeoutHTLC deliberately throws while the chain tip is below the HTLC timeout block, which is the normal case for a payment that just failed. So the rollback releases nothing, yet the failure result and the in-code comment ("stranded HTLCs are never left behind silently") imply it did.
findings.impact: Liquidity stays locked until the timeout block, and callers have no state that says so. A retry can fail for lack of capacity that is not actually gone. This is a recovery-state and API-contract defect, not direct fund theft.

repro.expected: A failed payment records explicit refund-pending locks and releases them once the timeout is valid.
repro.actual: cancelHtlcs catches and ignores the "has not yet timed out" error; the caller sees only a failure.
evidence: fix proposed in PR #218 (pendingRefunds on failure; cancelPayment throws PendingRefundError)
packages/omnia-router/src/execute.ts:52 — try { await ops.timeoutHTLC(...) } catch { /* best-effort */ }
packages/omnia-router/src/execute.ts:68 — comment claims stranded HTLCs are never left behind

fix.approach: Persist refund-pending locks with their timeout blocks, expose that state in the payment result, and retry when the timeout becomes valid. Distinguish refunded from refund-pending rather than collapsing both into a generic failure.
constraints: Do not claim liquidity was released when timeoutHTLC threw.
Do not bypass the timeout guard to force an early release.
acceptance: A failed payment reports which locks remain pending and until which block.
A retry after the timeout block releases them.
The success path is unchanged.

findings.title: Relay link journal is not atomic and duplicate detection races the write
findings.source: security audit OMN-NEW-010, verified against source at 8fa26907
findings.summary: record() writes the link, then reads the index, then writes the index as a separate operation with no transaction or compare-and-swap. Two concurrent forwards for the same hashlock both pass the duplicate check (which runs before record) and can then both record, with the second index write overwriting the first.
findings.impact: A lost index update hides a link from list()-based recovery, and a duplicate forward creates two outgoing HTLCs for one incoming payment. Both are restart-sensitive and hard to see in logs.

repro.expected: Journal writes are atomic and an incoming HTLC has a single idempotency key.
repro.actual: Two sequential storage.set calls per record; duplicate check precedes the write.
evidence: fix proposed in PR #218 (single-document journal, serialized, upsert by hashlock)

fix.approach: Use one atomic write per link (store the index inside the record, or use a storage transaction), and key idempotency on inChannelId+inHtlcId with a conditional insert. Recover from authoritative records, not from a separately maintained index.
constraints: Do not require a storage adapter feature the published adapters do not have.
Keep list() working for adapters that already hold data.
acceptance: Concurrent record() calls for the same hashlock produce exactly one entry and one outgoing HTLC.
A crash between the two writes cannot lose the link.

findings.title: Funding change goes to the first input owner, and the builder accepts negative output amounts
findings.source: security audit OMN-NEW-011, verified against source at 8fa26907
findings.summary: The CAN-001 fix returns change correctly for a single-owner coin, but two edges remain. With several funding inputs, all excess value is sent to inputAddresses[0] even when the inputs belong to different addresses. In tx-builder, amounts are summed per token and checked against the inputs, but individual negative amounts are never rejected, so a negative output can offset a positive one and still balance.
findings.impact: Multi-owner funding pays the change to the wrong party (and the transaction then cannot be signed by that party alone, so it fails late). The negative-amount gap means a draft can carry an invalid coin amount through conservation checking. Node acceptance of such a transaction was not demonstrated.

repro.expected: Change is returned per input owner, and every amount is required to be a non-negative integer before conservation is evaluated.
repro.actual: Change uses inputAddresses[0] unconditionally; sums() accepts BigInt("-100") and only compares totals.
evidence: fix proposed in PR #218 (mixed-owner funding rejected; negative amounts refused)
packages/tx-builder/src/build.ts:119 — sums() parses amounts with BigInt without a sign check
packages/tx-builder/src/build.ts:136 — only total > available is rejected

fix.approach: Require all funding inputs to share an owner before emitting change, or emit one change output per input address and reject mixed-owner funding with a clear error. In the builder, reject any amount that is negative or not an integer before summing.
constraints: Keep the single-input exact-value path byte-identical.
Do not weaken the existing conservation check.
acceptance: Mixed-owner funding either produces per-owner change or is rejected explicitly.
An output with a negative amount is rejected by the builder.
Offsetting positive and negative outputs cannot pass conservation.

findings.title: Watchtower starts but only observes; it never contests, fulfils or refunds
findings.source: re-audit R-004, verified against source at 5d8c427b
findings.summary: CAN-014 wired the watch service into host start/close and stopped it mistaking updates for closes. Its host callbacks, however, only emit observations: no contest transaction, no HTLC fulfilment or timeout, no refund. A successful close notification also adds the channel to the processed set even though nothing protective ran.
findings.impact: A unilateral close is detected but not answered before the contest deadline, so detection does not protect funds. The processed set can suppress later findings for a channel that is still at risk.

repro.expected: A detected close triggers the protective action and records evidence of completion.
repro.actual: onUnilateralClose emits an observation and the channel is then marked processed.
evidence: packages/omnia-host/src/watch.ts — closed set updated after the callback resolves

fix.approach: Give the watch service a durable response state machine: explicit contest/fulfil/refund actions, deadline tracking, retries and completion evidence. Only mark a channel processed when the action succeeded.
constraints: Do not mark processed on observation alone.
Do not automate actions the custody mode forbids.
acceptance: A simulated unilateral close produces a contest action before the deadline.
A failed action is retried and never marked complete.
Restart resumes pending responses.

findings.title: Prepared operations bypass the channel lock; refunds are not surfaced by the host; journal is not cross-process safe
findings.source: re-audit R-005, verified against source at 5d8c427b
findings.summary: Three related gaps remain. (1) The shared lock keys on params.channelId, so prepared operations that identify the work by preparedOperationId do not take it (and multi-channel work has no ordered locking). (2) The router now returns pendingRefunds, but the host multi-hop method throws on failure instead of returning that recovery information, and nothing persists a refund queue. (3) The relay journal is a single document per process, but has no storage-level compare-and-swap and does not serialize by incoming HTLC identity.
findings.impact: Concurrent prepared operations can interleave with RPC/peer mutations on the same channel; a failed multi-hop payment loses the refund schedule at the host boundary; two relay processes can lose a journal update.

repro.expected: Prepared, RPC and peer mutations share one lock; failures carry refunds; journal writes are atomic across processes.
repro.actual: Lock lookup ignores preparedOperationId; host throws the router result away; journal has no CAS.
evidence: packages/omnia-host/src/api/methods.ts:3342-3358 — lock key derived only from params.channelId
packages/omnia-router/src/execute.ts — pendingRefunds returned to the caller
packages/omnia-host/src/api/methods.ts — multi-hop handler throws without surfacing pendingRefunds
packages/omnia-relay/src/link-journal.ts — single document, no CAS or per-incoming-key lock

fix.approach: Resolve the channel from the prepared operation before taking the lock; sort multi-channel locks by channelId to avoid deadlock; return pendingRefunds from the host multi-hop method and persist a refund queue; add a compare-and-swap to the journal (revision field) and an idempotency key on inChannelId+inHtlcId.
constraints: Do not serialize unrelated channels.
Do not report a failure as fully refunded.
acceptance: A prepared submission and an RPC call on one channel cannot interleave.
Host multi-hop failures carry pendingRefunds and a scheduled retry.
Concurrent journal writers cannot lose an update.

findings.title: EpochAuthority.append is check-then-act across an await
findings.summary: append() reads current state, checks `spentInputIds`, then awaits `journal.append`. Two concurrent appends for the same input can both pass the check before either writes.
findings.impact: The same VTXO input can be recorded in two epochs, defeating the double-spend guard the journal is meant to provide. Realistic only under concurrent callers in one process or two processes sharing the journal.

repro.expected: Two concurrent appends of the same input: exactly one succeeds.
repro.actual: Both can pass the spent-input check before either append lands.

fix.approach: Use an atomic reservation (compare-and-swap on the journal head, or a per-authority serial queue) so the spent set is advanced in the same durable step as the append.
constraints: Do not add a process-local mutex as the only guard; two processes must still be safe.
Preserve the existing signature and epoch ordering checks.
acceptance: Two concurrent appends of the same input: one wins, one throws.
Reopen still shows a single record.

findings.title: Channel graphs advertise every channel that is not closed
findings.summary: The routing provider filters `channel.status === 'closed'`, so funding_pending, quiesced and spliced channels are advertised as routable even though HTLC creation requires `active`. A path can be selected and then fail at lock time.
findings.impact: Routes fail late, after a payment has been attempted; in-flight payments can be stranded.

repro.expected: Only `active` channels appear in the routing graph.
repro.actual: Every status except `closed` is advertised.

fix.approach: Filter on the positive predicate (`active`) instead of excluding one terminal status, and share the predicate with the HTLC entry check.
constraints: Do not change channel status values or the wire format.
Spliced channels must rejoin the graph when they return to active.
acceptance: A graph built from mixed-status channels contains only active ones.
A channel that returns to active is routable again.

findings.title: createMultiHopForwarder is exported but never instantiated by the host
findings.summary: The forwarding engine exists in omnia-relay and is exported, but no production host path constructs it. Multi-hop forwarding therefore depends on wiring that the reviewed host does not demonstrate.
findings.impact: The relay package appears supported while the deployed host cannot forward; a two-hop payment has no executing component.

repro.expected: A host started with relay enabled constructs the forwarder and drives it from the channel event stream.
repro.actual: Only the export exists; no host call site.

fix.approach: Either wire the forwarder into the host lifecycle with a durable journal and expose its state, or mark the package explicitly as a library primitive and remove the implied host support from docs and claims.
constraints: Do not advertise multi-hop as available while it is unwired.
If wired, the journal must be the durable one from OMN-006.
acceptance: Either the host constructs the forwarder and passes an integration test, or the docs and package maturity state that it is library-only.

findings.title: Link journal serialization is in-process only
findings.summary: Journal updates are serialized within one process. The duplicate-forward check runs before signing, so two processes sharing a store can both reserve the same payment.
findings.impact: Two relay processes can both forward one incoming HTLC, producing a double settlement attempt.

repro.expected: Two processes competing for the same hashlock: one forward.
repro.actual: No cross-process reservation.

fix.approach: Reserve atomically in the shared store (CAS on a per-hashlock key) before signing, and release on failure.
constraints: Do not rely on a process-local mutex.
A crashed reservation must be reclaimable after a bounded lease.
acceptance: Two processes: exactly one reservation succeeds.
Expired reservations are reclaimable without double settlement.

findings.title: Channel locking is keyed by the RPC channelId and multi-channel paths escape it
findings.summary: withChannelLock is applied where a channelId is present, but prepared-operation and multi-channel paths can touch several channels without entering a common critical section. Locking on a caller-supplied id also lets a caller serialize against the wrong key.
findings.impact: Concurrent operations on the same channel can interleave through a path that did not take the lock.

repro.expected: Any handler that mutates channel state holds a lock keyed by the channel it derives, not the request.
repro.actual: Some paths take no lock or use the request channelId.

fix.approach: Derive lock keys from the resolved channel(s), take them in a stable order for multi-channel operations, and cover prepared-operation commits.
constraints: No deadlock: multi-channel locks must be ordered.
Re-entrancy must keep working.
acceptance: A concurrent test over the same channel cannot interleave.
A multi-channel operation takes both locks in a deterministic order.

findings.title: Factory escape block is derived from the local chain tip
findings.summary: buildFactoryOpening computes `escapeBlock = tip.block + FACTORY_ESCAPE_DELAY_BLOCKS` and puts it in the funding script, while the pending commitment excludes it. Two hosts at different heights therefore derive different scripts for the same proposal, and the finalized terms comparison rejects the opening.
findings.impact: Factories fail to open whenever participants are not at the same tip. This is a liveness defect, not a divergence: the differing script is detected rather than silently accepted.

repro.expected: Both participants derive the same funding script and identity from a proposal.
repro.actual: escapeBlock differs with the tip, so fundingScript and fundingAddress differ.
evidence: packages/omnia-factory/src/factory.ts: pendingCommitment built without state variables

fix.approach: Derive the escape block from an agreed anchor (the proposal carries it, or it is the funding coin height) and commit to it in the pending commitment so a mismatch is impossible rather than merely detected.
constraints: Do not weaken the escape delay.
The commitment must cover every script-affecting input.
acceptance: Two hosts at different tips derive the same funding script from one proposal.
A changed escape block changes the commitment.

findings.title: Repeated settlement requests can exhaust WOTS signing capacity
findings.summary: The peer settlement handler called signSettlementRequest on every matching request, allocating a fresh lease even for identical channel/sequence/digest. A replay cache keyed by channel/sequence/digest now reuses the response and rejects a conflicting settlement for the same sequence, with an optional durable store wired to the host state store. A dedicated regression test and full durable approval policy remain.
findings.impact: A counterparty could previously consume one-time signing capacity without completing a settlement.

repro.expected: Identical requests reuse the stored co-signature; conflicting requests are rejected.
repro.actual: Replay defense implemented in integration.ts; regression test still to add.

fix.approach: Persist the signed response by canonical digest+participant, return the same response for idempotent retries, reject conflicting requests, and enforce a bounded signing policy.
constraints: Do not burn a leaf for a replayed request.
Reject a different settlement for the same channel+sequence.
acceptance: Repeat request returns the same signature.
Conflicting request is rejected.
Durable store survives restart.

findings.title: VTXO transfer verification omits value and recipient binding
findings.summary: verifyVtxoTransfer now requires a positive amount, binds from/to to the input/output owners, requires output.amount === transfer.amount, checks pool/token on the transfer record, and requires change with exact conservation for partial transfers.
findings.impact: A standalone transfer record can no longer verify while describing a different recipient, amount or pool than the supplied output.

repro.expected: Mismatched owner/amount/pool/token or a partial transfer without change is rejected.
repro.actual: Fixed in verifyVtxoTransfer.

fix.approach: Enforce exact amount and owner binding, positive values, token/pool binding and conservation with change, while keeping the authoritative double-spend/operator-signature checks separate.
constraints: Do not conflate this helper with the authoritative operator check.
acceptance: Wrong owner/amount/pool is rejected.
Partial transfer requires change and conserves value.

findings.title: Live liquidity allocation targets were exposed but not wired to execution
findings.summary: allocatePositionCapital requires an execution context for channel/factory/router/VTXO targets, but the host RPC called it without one, so only reserve worked. The host now builds the router and VTXO ports from its own state, accepts injected channel/factory ports, and rejects any target it cannot execute before accounting is touched.
findings.impact: Advertised allocation types failed through the host API; the unit test covered only reserve.

repro.expected: Every advertised target executes with its execution port or is rejected at request validation.
repro.actual: Fixed: router/VTXO execute; channel/factory require injected ports; unknown targets are rejected.

fix.approach: Inject live execution ports, execute each target, and fail validation before any accounting mutation.
constraints: Do not advertise unsupported targets.
Accounting is only updated after execution succeeds.
acceptance: Router and VTXO targets execute end-to-end.
An unconfigured channel target is rejected without accounting changes.

findings.title: Unauthenticated route advertisements could poison the routing graph
findings.summary: The host accepted ROUTE_GRAPH_ANNOUNCE edges without checking that the announcer participates in the claimed channel or that the channel exists, then merged them into the live router. Announcements are now authenticated against local channels, endpoints and token are bound to that channel, economic fields are clamped to real capacity, size and age are bounded, and only authenticated edges are re-gossiped.
findings.impact: A peer could advertise nonexistent capacity and make route discovery return unusable paths.

repro.expected: Announcements are authenticated and validated against real channels.
repro.actual: Fixed: unknown channels, foreign announcers, inflated capacity and oversized batches are ignored.

fix.approach: Authenticate announcements, bind them to real channel participants, clamp economic fields, bound age/size, and re-gossip only authenticated edges.
constraints: Do not treat unverified advertisements as executable capacity.
acceptance: Unknown or foreign channel announcements are ignored.
Inflated capacity is clamped.
Oversized batches are dropped.

findings.title: Explicit splice balance maps were not converted at the RPC boundary
findings.summary: Both splice handlers passed newBalances straight through with a type assertion, so decimal strings reached bigint arithmetic. Both now use the shared amount-record converter with participant-key validation.
findings.impact: A JSON request with decimal balances failed conservation arithmetic.

repro.expected: Decimal newBalances are converted to atoms.
repro.actual: Fixed: amountRecord() is used for splice-in and splice-out.

fix.approach: Convert and validate explicit balance maps at the RPC boundary.
constraints: Keys must match the participant set; balances non-negative.
acceptance: Decimal balance maps are accepted.
Unknown keys are rejected.

findings.title: Channel capacity warnings ignore the host shared physical WOTS tree
findings.summary: enforceUpdateGuards estimates consumption as newSequence * 2 for the channel alone. The host maps every logical tree label onto one physical tree, so many healthy-looking channels can exhaust the shared 4,096-leaf budget together with factory and receipt signing.
findings.impact: Availability and capacity planning: true exhaustion is still refused by the lease provider, so this is not key reuse.

repro.expected: Capacity warnings derive from the physical lease provider's consumed/reserved leaves.
repro.actual: Warnings are computed per channel from the sequence number only.

fix.approach: Feed actual lease usage into the capacity decision and budget per existing channel plus recovery requirements.
constraints: Keep failing closed on true exhaustion.
Do not weaken the per-channel double-sign guard.
acceptance: A host nearing physical exhaustion warns before signing.
A single channel cannot mask shared-tree pressure.

findings.title: Factory funding omitted the participant-root commitment its script pins
findings.summary: The funding covenant asserts SAMESTATE over STATE(111)/STATE(112), but the funding output seeded neither root. Deterministic party and balance roots are now computed and seeded, and exposed on the opening plan.
findings.impact: The advertised on-chain proof commitment was absent from the normal creation path.

repro.expected: Funding seeds STATE(111) and STATE(112).
repro.actual: Fixed: both roots are computed and seeded.

fix.approach: Compute canonical roots and bind them into the funding state.
constraints: The roots must be recomputable by any verifier.
acceptance: Ports 111/112 carry the roots.
Tampering changes the commitment.

findings.title: Rust/WASM CHECKSIG cannot verify a tree signature (the on-chain form)
findings.summary: core-wasm had no byte reader for TreeSignature, so the Rust/WASM evaluator could only verify the flat WOTS form. core-wasm now implements deserialize_tree_signature (Minima Signature.readDataStream layout) and the Rust CHECKSIG branch tries the canonical tree signature first, falling back to flat WOTS. TypeScript and Rust/WASM agree on every fixture.
findings.impact: A covenant verifying an oracle or recovery certificate now behaves identically in both evaluators instead of failing closed only in the WASM build.

repro.expected: TS and WASM both verify a canonical tree signature over the supplied data.
repro.actual: Fixed: the WASM evaluator reports CHECKSIG(tree …) and matches the TypeScript verdict on all fixtures.

fix.approach: Add a MiniData byte reader for TreeSignature in core-wasm (matching Signature.convertMiniDataVersion), use it in the Rust CHECKSIG branch, rebuild both wasm targets, and promote the pending fixtures.
constraints: Do not accept a flat signature where the node expects a tree signature.
Keep TS and Rust byte-identical on the same fixtures.
acceptance: The tree-signature fixtures pass in TS and WASM.
The parity suite has no pending-tree-signature entries (guarded).
The node leg (scripts/kissvm-node-parity.mjs) agrees when run against a node.

findings.title: 41 publishable packages declare no test:integration gate
findings.summary: The maturity gate requires test:integration for RC packages, but these declare none and carry no reasoned notApplicable exemption. They are invisible to `verify-workspace --integration`.
findings.impact: A behavioural regression in any of these packages reaches a release with no integration evidence; the canary cannot cover them all on its own.

repro.expected: Every RC package either declares test:integration or a reasoned exemption.
repro.actual: Missing: @totemsdk/agent-policy (rc), @totemsdk/authority (rc), @totemsdk/chain-provider (rc), @totemsdk/connect (rc), @totemsdk/decision (beta), @totemsdk/edge (rc), @totemsdk/governance (rc), @totemsdk/identity (rc), @totemsdk/intelligence (beta), @totemsdk/kissvm (rc), @totemsdk/liquidity-bond (rc), @totemsdk/lookup-client (rc), @totemsdk/lookup-node (rc), @totemsdk/lookup-protocol (rc), @totemsdk/manifest (rc), @totemsdk/mcp-server (rc), @totemsdk/omnia-factory (rc), @totemsdk/omnia-host (rc), @totemsdk/omnia-pool (rc), @totemsdk/omnia-router (rc), @totemsdk/omnia-vtxo (rc), @totemsdk/p2p-hub (alpha), @totemsdk/pear (rc), @totemsdk/provider-bond (rc), @totemsdk/minima-rpc (rc), @totemsdk/pubsub-transport (rc), @totemsdk/qvac (beta), @totemsdk/realtime (rc), @totemsdk/recursive-mast (rc), @totemsdk/root-identity (rc), @totemsdk/se-server (rc), @totemsdk/server (rc), @totemsdk/storage (rc), @totemsdk/stream-transport (rc), @totemsdk/tx-builder (rc), @totemsdk/txpow (rc), @totemsdk/wallet-adapter (rc), @totemsdk/wots-lease (rc), @totemsdk/entity (alpha), @totemsdk/eefi (rc), @totemsdk/replication (alpha)

where: the packages listed in this finding
fix.approach: Add a real test:integration per package (packed-consumer or invariant check), or record a reasoned notApplicable exemption in scripts/workspace-gates.config.json naming an owner.
constraints: Do not add notApplicable entries without an owner and a reason.
Do not add a script that always exits 0.
acceptance: node scripts/verify-workspace.mjs --integration reports no missing test:integration for RC packages.
Each new suite asserts behaviour, not just an import.

findings.title: Two unit suites exceed Jest's 5s default timeout under load
findings.source: canary core exercise: omnia-host prepare-submit-settle, lookup-node lease
findings.summary: The full unit suites fail on a loaded machine because individual tests inherit the 5,000 ms default. omnia-host prepareSettle/submitSettle takes ~15s end to end; lookup-node LEASE_RESERVE passes in 3s alone but exceeds 5s inside the 108s suite. Both pass when given 60s.
findings.impact: CI flakiness and false reds: the suites are green on a fast runner and red on a busy one, so a real regression and a slow machine look identical. It also blocks the canary from exercising these packages as part of a full run.

repro.expected: Both suites pass deterministically.
repro.actual: omnia-host: 1 failed / 125 passed (Exceeded timeout of 5000 ms). lookup-node: 1 failed / 70 passed. Both pass with --testTimeout=60000.
evidence: rerun with --testTimeout=60000: 1 passed / 125 skipped, and 1 passed / 70 skipped

fix.approach: Give the specific long tests an explicit timeout that reflects their work (settlement signing and a real lease round-trip), rather than raising the default for every test in the repo.
constraints: Do not set a repo-wide 60s default; it hides genuine hangs.
Do not skip or retry the tests.
acceptance: The full suites pass twice in a row on a loaded machine.
The timeout is scoped to the tests that need it, with a comment saying why.

findings.title: Auto-approval has no mandatory bound (hardening, not a defect)
findings.summary: The gate is deny-by-default and supports both `maxTotalValue` and `allowedPeers`, and both are enforced. `autoApprove: true` with neither bound is still permitted, so an operator can opt into unbounded signing.
findings.impact: A misconfigured unattended host can sign any factory a peer asks for. The default configuration is safe.

repro.expected: Enabling auto-approval without a bound is rejected at construction.
repro.actual: It is accepted; every request is then allowed.

fix.approach: Require at least one bound when `autoApprove` is set, and log the effective policy at startup. Keep the existing defaults and the authorizer hook unchanged.
constraints: Do not change the default-deny behaviour.
Do not make an explicit operator authorizer require the bounds.
acceptance: `autoApprove` without `maxTotalValue` or `allowedPeers` throws at construction.
A bounded policy still auto-approves within its bounds.

origin.note: Downgraded from P2: the gate is deny-by-default and both bounds exist and are enforced. The residual issue is that an operator may opt into auto-approval without a bound; that is configuration hardening, not the unbounded-automation defect the report describes.
